name: Unreliable Mobile Networks
intent: Design the client and the API for links that drop, stall and change under the user: timeouts that follow the network, retries with backoff, jitter and a budget, idempotency keys, fewer and smaller requests, and a radio that is not woken for every call.
scenario: A home screen needs 12 small requests; the first 4 make it usable. On a link that loses 10% of attempts with a 300 ms round trip, a client that loads them one after another with a fixed 1,000 ms timeout is usable after 6,780 ms, sends 15 requests and wakes the radio 12 times. A parallel client with backoff and jitter needs 1,850 ms and 1 wake-up, and one batched request needs 540 ms. Then 10,000 phones reconnect after an outage at once.
problem: A phone moves from Wi-Fi to cellular, goes through a tunnel, sits at the edge of a cell. Latency is high and varies from one request to the next, connections die silently, and a request can fail after the server has already done the work. Code written against an office network, with a fixed timeout, an immediate retry and a dozen chatty calls, then loads slowly, drains the battery, double-charges a customer, and when many phones come back at once after an outage, floods the recovering server with synchronised retries.

howItWorks.title: Make the timeout fit the network
howItWorks.text: A timeout that is shorter than the real round trip makes every attempt fail, and the retries only add load. A timeout that is far too long leaves the user waiting on a dead connection. Choose the timeout from what you measure on that link, such as a multiple of the recent round-trip time, and give the whole screen a deadline as well as each request, so a stalled call does not outlast the user's patience.

howItWorks.title: Retry with backoff, jitter and a budget
howItWorks.text: A failed request is retried after a pause that grows with each attempt (exponential backoff), with a random component (jitter) so that thousands of phones do not retry at the same instant. A retry budget caps the total retries of a client, so a bad link does not turn one screen into dozens of requests. Retry only what is safe to retry, and give up with a clear message instead of retrying for ever.

howItWorks.title: Make a retried write safe
howItWorks.text: A request can time out after the server has applied it, so the client cannot know whether it succeeded. Send an idempotency key with each write, a unique id the server remembers, so a repeat returns the first result instead of charging, posting or creating twice. This is what turns 'retry on failure' from a risk into a rule.

howItWorks.title: Send less, and fewer times
howItWorks.text: Every round trip pays the full latency, and every small request can wake the radio. Combine the calls a screen needs into one request or a few (a batch, or an endpoint shaped for that screen), compress the bodies, send only the fields the screen uses, cache what changes rarely, and fetch ahead while on Wi-Fi. A big batch has a cost: a larger reply is more exposed to loss and is all-or-nothing, so keep batches modest and let the server return partial results.

howItWorks.title: Expect the whole fleet to come back together
howItWorks.text: After an outage or a long tunnel, many clients become able to connect at the same moment. If they all retry on the same schedule, the server sees a spike every backoff interval and may never recover. Add jitter to the reconnect itself and to every retry delay, honour a retry-after hint when the server sends one, and let the server shed load with a quick error instead of queueing requests it cannot serve.

pros: The app loads in a usable state sooner on slow and lossy links, and shows something instead of failing
Fewer requests and fewer radio wake-ups save battery and data
Backoff with jitter and a budget keep a client from hurting a server that is already struggling
Idempotency keys make retries safe for writes, so users are not charged or posted to twice
cons: More client logic: timeouts, retry rules, queues and cancellation all have to be written and tested
Batching couples calls together, so one slow or failing part can delay the rest unless the server returns partial results
Retries and caches can show stale or late data, so the interface has to say what it is showing
Testing needs bad networks on purpose, which a developer's office Wi-Fi never provides
whenToUse: Any app used on mobile data, in motion or in places with weak coverage
Screens that fan out into many small calls, and clients that poll or sync often
Services that many phones will reconnect to at once, after an outage, a push or a scheduled sync
whenNotToUse: A fixed timeout and an immediate retry loop, as a default, on any link that is not a datacentre network
Retrying calls that are not idempotent, with no key to make them safe
Batching so much into one request that a single failure throws away everything
pitfalls: A fixed timeout shorter than the round trip, so every attempt fails and the app sends the same requests again and again
Retrying immediately or on a fixed schedule, so all clients come back in step
No retry budget or deadline, so a bad link multiplies requests instead of failing fast
Retrying a POST without an idempotency key
Firing many small requests spread over time, so the radio never goes idle
Treating 'online' from the OS as 'the server is reachable': a connected phone can still have a dead link

roles.label: User
roles.description: Moves between Wi-Fi, cellular and no signal while using the app.

roles.label: Mobile client
roles.description: Sets timeouts, retries, batches requests and decides when to use the radio.

roles.label: Radio
roles.description: Uses much more power when it wakes up for a transfer, and stays awake for a while after.

roles.label: Flaky link
roles.description: Loses attempts and varies in latency.

roles.label: Server
roles.description: Applies each idempotency key once and can reject requests when overloaded.

quiz.question: A mobile client uses a fixed 1,000 ms timeout and retries at once. A user on a slow connection has a round trip of 1,200 ms. What happens?
options: Each attempt eventually succeeds, because the retry gives the link more time.
The server rejects the requests as duplicates, so none are processed.
The retries succeed on the second try, since the first one warms the connection.
Every attempt times out before its reply arrives, so the screen never loads and the traffic is wasted.
quiz.explanation: A reply that normally takes longer than the timeout can never arrive in time, so each retry fails the same way and adds load. The timeout has to follow the measured round trip, and retries need backoff and a limit.

quiz.question: A phone sends a payment request and the connection drops before the reply. The app retries. What makes that safe?
options: A longer timeout on the retry, so the first reply can still arrive.
An idempotency key sent with both attempts, which the server uses to return the first result.
Retrying only on Wi-Fi, where requests never time out.
Sending the retry from a different device, so the server treats it as new.
quiz.explanation: After a timeout the client cannot know whether the server applied the payment. The same key on every attempt lets the server recognise a repeat and answer with the original outcome instead of charging again.

quiz.question: 10,000 phones regain signal at the same moment after an outage. Each retries a failed request after 1 s, then 2 s, then 4 s. Why does the server keep being overloaded?
options: Exponential delays are too short to give a server time to recover.
The server counts each phone's retries and refuses to answer a phone twice.
The delays are identical on every phone, so all the retries still arrive in the same second.
Backoff only works with a retry limit of one attempt.
quiz.explanation: Backoff spaces out one client's retries but does nothing to spread many clients apart if they start together and use the same delays. A random component (jitter) on the reconnect and on each delay turns the spikes into a steady trickle.
